title: The deepest hole
teaches: Project Mohole, the Kola Superdeep Borehole and KTB: what drilling into the crust found, and why the holes stopped

parts.title: A drill ship with no anchor

blocks.text: Everything in this branch so far was learned at a distance, from gravity and from waves. In 1957 a group of American scientists, including the oceanographer Walter Munk and the geologist Harry Hess of lesson 9, asked why no one had simply drilled through the crust and brought back a piece of the mantle. Their informal club, the American Miscellaneous Society, proposed **Project Mohole**: a hole to the Moho.

They chose the ocean. Lesson D3 showed that ocean crust is only about 7 kilometres thick, against 30 to 50 under the continents. The difficulty was that the sea floor there is several kilometres under water. In March and April 1961 a converted oil-drilling barge, CUSS I, drilled at a site in water 3,560 metres deep off Guadalupe Island, Mexico. It had no anchor that could reach the bottom; instead four outboard motors, steered by a crew watching sonar and radar markers, held the ship over the hole, the first use of what is now called dynamic positioning. The drill went 183 metres into the sea floor and its last few metres were basalt, the first sample ever taken of the ocean's crust. The novelist John Steinbeck was aboard to write about it for *Life* magazine.

blocks.caption: The drilling barge CUSS I, used for the first phase of Project Mohole in 1961.

blocks.text: That was as deep as Mohole went. The next phase was meant to need a much larger ship, and the project became mired in disputes over contractors and cost. Congress cancelled it in 1966. But its methods survived: the Deep Sea Drilling Project's ship *Glomar Challenger* began work in 1968 and drilled hundreds of shallow holes across the oceans, recovering the sediments that confirmed the sea floor gets older away from the ridges (lesson 9).

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Project Mohole (proposed 1957) aimed to drill through the thin ocean crust to the Moho.
In 1961 CUSS I drilled 183 m into the sea floor in 3,560 m of water, holding position without anchors, and recovered basalt.
Mohole was cancelled in 1966, but its methods led to the scientific ocean drilling that confirmed seafloor spreading.

blocks.text: The Soviet Union chose a different route: drill on land, where the work is easier, and go as deep as possible. On 24 May 1970, on the Kola Peninsula in the far northwest of Russia, near the Norwegian border, drilling began on a hole designated SG-3. The site sits on the Baltic Shield, a region of very old, hard crystalline rock, some of it more than 2.5 billion years old. The goal was 15 kilometres.

Drilling that deep needs a new approach. A string of steel pipe 12 kilometres long cannot be spun from the top without twisting itself apart, so the Kola team kept the pipe still and drove the bit with a turbine at the bottom, powered by drilling mud pumped down the pipe. The pipe was made of aluminium alloy to save weight. Each time the bit wore out, which in deep hard rock was every few hours of drilling, the whole string had to be pulled up, unscrewed in sections and lowered again, which took many hours. The hole was 23 centimetres across. In 1989 it reached 12,262 metres, the deepest hole ever drilled, a record it still holds.

blocks.caption: The Kola Superdeep Borehole site in 2007, after drilling had stopped.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The Kola Superdeep Borehole (SG-3) began in 1970 in ancient rock of the Baltic Shield, aiming for 15 km.
It used a turbine at the bottom of the hole instead of spinning the whole string of pipe.
It reached 12,262 m in 1989, still the deepest hole ever drilled.

blocks.text: Kola was drilled partly to test what seismology said. Refraction surveys of the kind in lesson D3 showed a boundary at about 7 kilometres where wave speeds increased, and the textbook interpretation was that granite gave way to basalt there. The drill found no basalt. Below 7 kilometres the rock was still granite and gneiss (a banded metamorphic rock, lesson 5). The seismic boundary was the top of a zone where those rocks had been altered by heat and pressure and were cracked and filled with water. The lesson for geologists was that a change in wave speed marks a change in rock properties, which is not necessarily a change in rock type.

That water was the second surprise. The rock at several kilometres down was expected to be dry and tight. Instead it was fractured and wet, with water that had been squeezed out of minerals and trapped beneath impermeable rock above. The drilling mud came back up bubbling with hydrogen and other gases. And in cores from about 6 kilometres down, Soviet scientists reported microscopic fossils of single-celled plankton, 24 species of them, preserved in carbon and nitrogen compounds rather than replaced by stone.

blocks.caption: Rock cores from a borehole, laid out in boxes in order of depth.

blocks.text: The third surprise stopped the project. Temperatures had been predicted to reach about 100 °C at 12 kilometres. The rock at the bottom was about 180 °C. At that temperature, and under that pressure, the rock was weaker and behaved more like a stiff plastic than a brittle solid; the walls of the hole crept inward, and every time the bit was pulled out, the hole began to close. Equipment failed faster in the heat. After several attempts to push deeper ended in lost and stuck pipe, drilling stopped in 1992. The hole was abandoned in 2008, and the opening is now covered with a welded steel cap.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Kola found no basalt where a seismic boundary had been read as granite giving way to basalt; the boundary was cracked, altered rock full of water.
It found water and gases deep in the crust, and reported microfossils from about 6 km.
The rock at the bottom was about 180 °C instead of the predicted 100 °C, and the hot rock crept into the hole.

blocks.text: Every deep hole meets the same limit. Rock gets hotter with depth, by about 25 °C per kilometre on average in continental crust (lesson 7's gradient from Kelvin's mines), and less in old, cold crust like Kola's. Drill bits, pipe, the mud and the instruments all have temperature limits, and hot rock under great pressure creeps into the hole. How deep a hole can go depends above all on how quickly the rock warms.

The German Continental Deep Drilling Program, KTB, tested this in Bavaria. A pilot hole reached 4,000 metres in 1989, and the main hole began in 1990 at Windischeschenbach, with the hope of passing 10 kilometres. The rock there warmed by nearly 28 °C per kilometre, almost twice Kola's rate. In 1994, at 9,101 metres, the temperature was 265 °C and the hole was stopped.

blocks.caption: Temperature against depth, for rock warming at the rate you set from a surface at 10 °C. The hole stops where the rock is hotter than the drill can stand. The real holes are marked; Kola's predicted temperature is the dotted line.
blocks.task: Find KTB’s depth from its rate of warming and its limit

blocks.caption: The KTB drilling rig at Windischeschenbach, Bavaria, one of the tallest land rigs ever built, at 83 metres.
The deepest hole against other depths and heights, on a scale where each mark is ten times the last.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Rock warms with depth, about 25 °C per km on average under continents.
Heat limits drilling: equipment fails and hot rock creeps into the hole.
KTB in Germany, in rock warming nearly 28 °C per km, stopped at 9,101 m and 265 °C in 1994.

blocks.text: The deepest hole on Earth reached about a third of the way to the Moho beneath it, and about one five-hundredth of the way to the centre. Holes for oil and gas have since been drilled longer than Kola, more than 12 kilometres, but they curve out sideways and do not go as deep.

The Mohole idea survives in the ocean. The drilling ship *JOIDES Resolution*, a descendant of *Glomar Challenger*, drilled for more than three decades, and Japan's larger ship *Chikyu*, built partly with the aim of reaching the mantle, has drilled into the sea floor since 2007. The deepest hole into ocean crust, Hole 504B off Ecuador, reached about 2.1 kilometres below the sea floor, still kilometres short of the Moho. In 2023 *JOIDES Resolution* took a different approach: on the Atlantis Massif in the mid-Atlantic, where a fault has brought mantle rock up to the sea floor, it drilled 1,268 metres into mantle peridotite and brought up the longest core of mantle rock yet.

blocks.caption: The drilling ship JOIDES Resolution, which drilled the sea floor for scientists from 1985 to 2024.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Kola went about a third of the way to the Moho under it.
Ocean drilling has not yet crossed the Moho; the deepest hole into ocean crust is about 2.1 km.
In 2023 a ship drilled 1,268 m into mantle rock exposed on the Atlantic sea floor by faulting.

blocks.caption: Six questions on deep drilling
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: Why did Project Mohole plan to drill in the ocean rather than on land?
choices: Ocean crust is only about 7 km thick, so the Moho is much nearer
Ocean rock is softer and easier to drill
Drilling on land was banned by treaty
items.why: Under continents the Moho is 30 to 50 km down; under the oceans it is about 7 km below the sea floor.

items.ask: What did Kola find at about 7 km, where seismologists had expected granite to give way to basalt?
choices: Still granite and gneiss, cracked, altered and full of water
A layer of basalt, as predicted
items.why: The seismic boundary marked a change in the rock's properties, not its type: fractured, altered rock filled with fluid.

items.ask: Why did drilling at Kola stop short of its 15 km goal?
choices: The rock was about 180 °C instead of the expected 100 °C, and the hot rock crept into the hole
items.why: At high temperature and pressure the rock behaved plastically and the hole kept closing, while equipment failed faster in the heat.

items.ask: KTB's rock warmed almost twice as fast with depth as Kola's. What did that mean for how deep it could go?
choices: It reached the drill's temperature limit sooner, and stopped at 9.1 km
It could go deeper, because hot rock is softer to drill
items.why: A steeper temperature gradient reaches any fixed limit at a shallower depth.

items.ask: How did CUSS I stay above its hole in water 3,560 m deep?
choices: Outboard motors, steered by crew watching sonar and radar markers, held it in place
It was tied to an oil platform
items.why: No anchor could reach the bottom. Holding position with steered propellers, now called dynamic positioning, was first done on Mohole.

items.ask: What was unusual about the 2023 Atlantis Massif hole?
choices: It drilled 1,268 m into mantle rock, brought near the sea floor by a fault
It was the first hole to cross the Moho
It was drilled from the Moon
items.why: The drill did not cross the Moho. A fault had brought mantle peridotite to the sea floor, so the drill could sample it directly.

learned: Project Mohole (1961) drilled 183 m into ocean crust from a drill ship held in place without anchors, and was cancelled in 1966.
The Kola Superdeep Borehole reached 12,262 m in 1989, finding unexpected water, no basalt layer, and rock at 180 °C.
Heat sets the limit: KTB stopped at 9,101 m and 265 °C.
No hole has reached the Moho; mantle rock has been drilled where faults bring it near the sea floor.
